name: Toki-shakuyaku-san (Kampo formula; Tang-Kuei-Shao-Yao-San in Chinese)
short: Pregnancy: no comparison with unexposed women; Japanese database: of 2,491 first-trimester-exposed infants, 12.5% preterm, 6.3% major malformations. Trials in other conditions: no severe side effects.
text: Names and herbs: a laboratory abstract gives Tang-Kuei-Shao-Yao-San as the Chinese name of Toki-shakuyaku-san, and a 1996 abstract lists its six herbs as peony root, Atractylodes lancea rhizome, Alisma rhizome, hoelen (Poria), Cnidium rhizome and Japanese angelica root. Trials (all small): in a prospective comparison in 25 women with anaemia from uterine fibroids, both preparations taken by mouth, side effects occurred in 80.0% of the 15 given an oral iron preparation and no significant side effects were observed in the 10 given the formula; no adverse events occurred in the 8 patients with mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease who completed an 8-week study; in a study in women with luteal insufficiency or normal menstrual cycles, no clinical side effects were detected; and in a randomized, non-blinded trial that enrolled 82 patients with loss of smell after infection, neither the formula nor vitamin B12 (mecobalamin), each given for 24 weeks, produced severe adverse events. Pregnancy: no study comparing pregnant women who took this formula with women who did not was found. In a Japanese claims-database study, women prescribed the formula in the first trimester served as the comparison group for another set of Kampo medicines: of 2,491 infants in this group, 311 (12.5%) were born preterm and 157 (6.3%) had major congenital malformations. That abstract gives no rate for women not taking Kampo medicines, so these figures cannot show whether the formula raises or lowers the risk. A pooled database study in hyperemesis gravidarum (observational), which included this formula among other Kampo medicines, found no significant differences in congenital anomalies, low birthweight or preterm birth among the groups, with no result for this formula alone. A Japanese database study reports that it was among the formulas most prescribed during pregnancy and says further research is needed on the relationship between Kampo use in pregnancy and adverse events in infants. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
